---
title: "Video microscopy and computer vision"
author: "Owen Petchey"
date: 2026-09-10
categories: [research, methods, video tracking, R]
image: cover.jpg
---

A microscope video of a protist microcosm contains far more information than a human observer can practically extract by eye: not just how many individuals of each species are present, but their body sizes, shapes, and how they're moving — all changing from one sampling point to the next. Getting that information out of raw video, reliably and at scale, needs computer vision rather than manual counting.

BEMOVI (BEhaviour and MOrphology from VIdeos) is an open-source video-analysis pipeline built for exactly this: it identifies individual organisms in each video frame, links them into trajectories across frames, and extracts per-individual measurements of body size, shape, and movement, alongside population-level metrics like density and size distributions. It was introduced in [Pennekamp, Schtickzelle & Petchey (2015), "BEMOVI, software for extracting behavior and morphology from videos, illustrated with analyses of microbes"](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/ece3.1529), and is [available on GitHub](https://github.com/efronhofer/bemovi) and at [bemovi.info](http://bemovi.info/).

This is what turns [experimental microbial ecology](../2026-09-11-experimental-microbial-ecology/index.qmd) from a source of jars and test tubes into a source of quantitative, repeated-measures data — the same kind of automated, non-invasive measurement that experiments testing ecological forecasts depend on.
